extracted.intended_audience: readers of Horace's Satires / students of classical literature (educated Roman audience; modern readers of Latin satire)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and framing the prescriptive/evaluative passages embedded in Horace's Satires (on madness, luxury, banqueting, inheritance-seeking, and country retirement) as explicit criteria or practical rules. The page is a literary/satirical text that contains many hortatory and advisory statements that function like practical precepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of wealth as a test of sanity (hoarding vs use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hoarding wealth without using it (guarding cash/gold, refusing to consume available provisions, letting bed-clothes rot unused) is a sign of madness and folly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace gives concrete examples (a man who watches over a heap of corn and won't take a single grain, one who keeps three hundred thousand but drinks only sharp vinegar, one who will not touch money as if consecrated). The text treats accumulation divorced from use as irrational—equate 'wealth unused' with delirium. Also illustrated by Opimius revived when his money-bags were poured out and counted: attachment to hoard is pathological.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covetousness ≠ soundness; moderation and absence of ambition required
rubrics_metrics.description: Not being covetous is necessary but not sufficient for soundness; a man free from avarice may still be unsound if he is ambitious, ostentatious, or otherwise immoderate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace notes that a man who is not perjured or sordid might still be 'ambitious and assuming' and that failing to use acquisitions (or obsessive desire to surpass others) is morally and mentally suspect. The advice is to prefer sufficiency and avoid ambition that seeks public honors (aedileship, praetorship), which are associated with loss of estate and madness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Luxury and ostentation as evidence of moral/mad behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Extravagant spendthrifts who stage massive displays, procure exotic fare, and pursue applause (e.g., for the circus or statues) are portrayed as mad and morally bankrupt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the youth who summons fishmongers, perfumers, buffoons each morning and dissolves pearls in vinegar to swallow them; brothers who dine on nightingales. Horace condemns living 'beyond your fortune' and seeking glory by wasteful largesse; such behavior is to be judged imprudent and foolish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish forms of madness (rage vs folly vs divinely driven frenzy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Madness may arise from different causes—blind rage, folly, or divine frenzy—and should be judged by its effects and objects; violent acts done under madness can be different in moral culpability than willful crimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace discusses Ajax (slaughtering sheep in madness but sparing family) and Orestes (madness driven by Furies), arguing one must consider whether delusion led to irreconcilable confusion of reality or to controlled violence. The criterion is whether the mind is 'disturbed' so as to form images foreign from reality and act under compulsion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love as childishness (behavioural immaturity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Being in love is likened to childish play and irrational behaviour—arguing with oneself, wandering to doors, invoking extremes—thus is treated as a form of folly rather than adult reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace compares excluded lovers to children building little houses and to those who vacillate by 'blind chance'; he characterizes love-driven actions as inherent evils lacking moderation and reason. The implicit evaluative standard: emotional self-possession and moderation are marks of sanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banqueting: ingredient selection and provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Good banqueting depends on selecting ingredients by origin and quality (e.g., oblong eggs preferred, cabbage from dry lands, meadow mushrooms, Lucrine muscles over Baian murex, best oysters from the Circaean promontory, crayfish from Misenum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace lists many origin-based preferences: oblong eggs as sweeter, Lucrine muscle preferable, Tarentum scallops prized, etc. The practical rule: know provenance and choose sources appropriate to each dish; quality is region-dependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banqueting: preparation techniques and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific cooking/preparation rules: tenderize tough hen in Falernian wine, use limpet and coarse cockles with Coan white wine to relieve a bound belly, finish dinners with black mulberries gathered before the sun, wash stomach with mead when needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace provides procedure-like instructions for making certain foods palatable and for restoring appetite. These are prescriptive, e.g., soaking a tough hen in Falernian to tenderize, or using particular shellfish to remove obstructions—apply the technique appropriate to the complaint or ingredient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wine handling, mixing, and sediment management
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for wines and blends: do not serve Massic in fair weather if it has thick parts unless it can be attenuated by nocturnal air; filtering through linen loses flavor; mix Surrentine with Falernian lees skillfully and collect sediment with a pigeon's egg (yolk sinks and rolls down with heterogeneous parts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace prescribes careful handling of wines and explicit mixing techniques; small technical measures (egg to collect lees) are recommended to preserve taste and clarity. The evaluative standard: preserve flavor and clarity while knowing when and how to blend wines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sauces, condiments, and pairing
rubrics_metrics.description: Know the two kinds of sauce (simple: sweet oil; complex: boiled shredded herbs with Corycian saffron and pressed Venafran olive berry) and appropriate pairings (which fish, roast, or pastry suits which sauce/seasoning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace emphasizes that mastery requires knowing which sauces suit stewed vs roasted fish and how herbs and saffron are applied. Also prescribes condiments like wine-lees and herring-brine with white pepper and black salt as tasteful combinations—attention to matching condiment to dish is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service, presentation, and hygiene in banqueting
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation and cleanliness matter: do not cramp roving fishes in narrow dishes, avoid servants with greasy hands touching cups, ensure trays/mats/sawdust (cheap items) are clean and attended, do not cover unwashed furniture with Tyrian carpets, and maintain clean floors and implements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace treats neglect of the cheap/ordinary accoutrements as a greater shame than extravagance where cleanliness is concerned. Practical rules include protecting cups from greasy hands, using appropriately sized dishes, and keeping serving surfaces clean.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banqueting philosophy: balance and holistic attention
rubrics_metrics.description: It is insufficient to focus on a single element (e.g., only the wine); an accomplished host attends to all parts of the meal—oil on fish, sauces, pastry, serving, and the overall harmony of the repast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace reproves those who spend lavishly on one item (fish market) but neglect others. The rule is holistic care: variety, proportion, and appropriateness across the entire banquet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of fortune‑hunters / tactics to secure an inheritance
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of repeated social and legal tactics to ingratiate oneself with rich old men for the sake of becoming heir: flatter openly, humor their tastes, act as solicitous companion, serve as their advocate in lawsuits (especially against better reputations), creep into second-heir positions, join with freedmen or 'cunning women', feign modesty about wills while peeking, praise their verses, perform attentions at funerals, and disguise joy when a bequest is favorable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace gives step-by-step behavioral advice—be complaisant but not overbearing, provide small personal services (guarding from crowds, praising), weep and feign emotion when appropriate, quietly observe any will-reading for advantageous clauses, and be ready to buy out co-heirs at a discount. These are ethically dubious social-engineering techniques described as practical craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performative comportment for ingratiation (posture, tone, timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: When cultivating a dependent relationship with an old man, adopt a carefully modulated comportment: neither too garrulous nor too silent, adopt occasional exaggerated humility (head on one side), weep sporadically, and manage visible emotion so as not to betray joy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace gives micro-advice on demeanor—speak enough to flatter but not offend, feign being moved to 'Enough' when praised, weep at key moments, disguise actual happiness at receiving a bequest. Timing and affect management are crucial to the craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Country retirement as criteria for a good life
rubrics_metrics.description: A desirable retirement consists of a modest plot with a garden, a fountain with constant stream, a little woodland, fattened cattle, and absence of evil ambition—valuing sufficiency, leisure, study, and convivial conversation over urban bustle and envy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace portrays the ideal as moderation and contentment: avoid the city's lawsuits, obligations, and envy; prefer evenings of simple feasts among friends where conversation is about what truly matters (virtue, happiness) rather than gossip about villas and spectacles.
